title: We Blame the Phone Because It Doesn't Implicate Us
author: Bauschard, Stefan
summary: I am long on the thing I say is poisoning my kids. That should be an uncomfortable sentence, and it is literally true. The index funds in my retirement account hold Meta, because nearly every index fund and pension and endowment in the country does. So the engagement model I'm morally short on, I'm financially long on. The teacher who confiscates phones at her classroom door has the attention economy in her 401(k). So does the school that made $24 million on Snapchat And it doesn't stop at the stock. I've handed my kids the tablet in the back seat because I wanted the twenty minutes of quiet, and I got it. I walked them through the mall and called it a treat. I've checked my email at the dinner table and then wondered, out loud, why they can't put their phones down. I'm starting here, in the dock, because the argument I want to make falls apart the second I exempt myself from it. We say social media broke our kids. It is always easier to externalize -- to find the thing out there that did this to us, rather than the thing in here that we did. And the cleanest version of that move, the one almost everyone reaches for, is the phone. So let me grant the phone everything its loudest critics want, up front, and then make my point anyway. Maybe it's an accelerant. Maybe it made things worse. I'll concede that and more in a minute. But the phone did not manufacture the anxiety, the status-hunger, the sense of a future that doesn't add up. It reflected those things back at a generation we had already shaped. The screen is a mirror. And the reason "ban it" is so satisfying is that smashing a mirror is so much easier than changing what it shows. Watch the script, because it runs the same way every time. A new machine arrives. The kids are suddenly "in crisis." And the cure is always to block the machine, and never to look at the room it walked into. Social media was the dress rehearsal. AI is opening night. Same play. Same casting. The only thing that changes is the name of the villain. The villain always changes, and paradise always recedes just behind it. Before the phone it was television. In 1961, the chairman of the FCC stood up in front of the broadcasters and called American television a "vast wasteland." Here's the part nobody remembers: that very speech was already mourning a lost golden age of TV -- the highbrow live drama of the 1950s, "the much bemoaned good old days," contrasted with the junk of 1961. The wasteland always has a garden right behind it. Before television it was comic books. In 1954 the United States Senate held actual hearings on whether comics were causing juvenile delinquency, anchored by a psychiatrist whose bestseller, Seduction of the Innocent , warned that the funny pages were corrupting a generation. It made the front page of the Times. It galvanized parents. It produced a censorship code. Before comics, it was the novel, rotting the minds of young women who read too much. There was never a year when school was working and a technology broke it. Every generation locates paradise just on the far side of the current villain. Which means we are not actually mourning something we lost. We are manufacturing something to have lost -- so that there is something, and someone, to blame. And here I have to be careful, because the dishonest version of this argument is as bad as the thing it's attacking. The answer to "was school awesome before the phone?" is not "school was a dystopia." That overshoots, and you know it does. Plenty of kids found a teacher who saw them, a team that held them, a stage where they became someone. I'm not interested in burning that down. The accurate charge is narrower and worse. School had chronic, named, unfixed failures -- and every one of them predates every villain we've ever blamed. The kid who ate lunch alone. The pressure that turned sleep into a luxury good. The curriculum built for a test instead of for a person. We knew about all of it. We wrote reports about all of it. We fixed approximately none of it. The kids, by the way, are not the broken thing in this story that needs repair. They are the readout. They are the honest instrument registering choices the adults made. We keep trying to recalibrate the instrument. Now the part we really don't want to look at. We cover their eyes at the feed and we walk them straight through the mall -- and the mall was engineered, on purpose, by people with research budgets, to do to the human mind precisely what we now accuse the app of doing. There is a name for it. The Gruen transfer : the moment a shopper, disoriented by an intentionally confusing layout, forgets what they came in for and starts buying on impulse. It is named for the architect of the modern mall. The bitter irony -- and it is the whole point -- is that he came to hate what developers did with his design, stuffing the floor with merchandise until disorientation itself became the product, because disoriented people spend more. Even the man who built the machine recoiled from it. We built it anyway. We live in it. We spend our Saturdays in it. The sugar at a four-year-old's eye level. The magazine rack at the checkout. The missing windows and missing clocks, so you lose track of time. None of it is an accident. All of it is the same desire-manufacture and attention-capture we suddenly find scandalous the instant it glows. Run it through the part that actually animates the panic about girls. The airbrushed, impossible female body did not arrive with Instagram. It was on every magazine cover, at every checkout, at child's-eye height, for the entire length of the childhoods of the very parents now horrified by the feed. We were raised inside the comparison machine. A lot of us metabolized it into our own lifelong bad relationships with the mirror. And then we walked our own daughters down the identical aisle and got scandalized only when the impossible bodies started arriving through a phone. So the outrage was never really about the mechanism. The mechanism is a century old. We built it, we profit from it, our retirement accounts are long on it, and we enjoy it on the weekend. We got upset when the engineering moved onto a device that felt like it belonged to them -- and to someone else. We police the version of the harm we can disown. If the harm itself were the thing that bothered us, the magazine rack would have provoked this fifty years ago. It didn't, because the magazine rack is ours. The phone we are allowed to hate, because we've coded it as not-ours. The wallet decides the outrage. Here is where I hand the other side its best card, because I'd rather lose a weak version of this argument than win one. The phone (really, social media) is not innocent, and I'm not going to pretend it is. The phone is the mall intensified -- personalized, infinite, never closes, and tuned by a model to find your specific wound and press on it. That's real, and it's new, and it's worse. And the single hardest fact for my side of this: the mental-health curves for adolescent girls bend at roughly the same moment across several countries, around 2012, and recession and bad curricula and consumer culture were all true before 2012. That synchronized timing is a genuine puzzle, and it is the strongest thing Jonathan Haidt has , and waving it away is not honest. Nor is the best evidence only correlational anymore. When economists exploited the staggered rollout of Facebook across U.S. college campuses -- a clean natural experiment, one campus switched on at a time -- they found it measurably worsened student mental health, depression most of all, apparently by feeding exactly the kind of unfavorable social comparison the magazine rack at the checkout was always selling. The mall went mobile, and you can see it in the data. And it is also true that the case is nowhere near as closed as the headlines insist. Candice Odgers, reviewing Haidt in Nature, called the alarm closer to a moral panic at a fevered pitch than a settled finding. Amy Orben and Andrew Przybylski, across hundreds of thousands of teenagers, found that screen use explains a fraction of a percent of the variation in well-being -- about the same as wearing glasses, or eating potatoes. The reviews piling up through 2025 mostly land in the uncomfortable middle: a small but fairly consistent association, working through many interacting pathways rather than one clean cause, with distress driving the scrolling about as much as the scrolling drives distress -- and the causal question still not closed. And then there's the one test this essay can't look away from. When researchers compared English schools that restrict phones against schools that don't, the bans showed no benefit -- not to mental health, not to sleep, not even to how much time kids spent on their phones overall -- even though that overall time still tracked with worse outcomes. Sit with that pairing. The single intervention we reach for first is the one piece of this whole debate we have come closest to proving doesn't work. The phone may well be hurting them. The ban still isn't helping. But notice -- I don't actually need to win that fight. That's the move. My claim isn't about what hurt them; that's a question the data may never resolve cleanly. My claim is about the order in which we agreed to look. Watch how fast we skipped past our own contribution -- the schools, the credential lie, the status culture, the mall we built -- to land on the one cause that doesn't implicate us. The externalization doesn't show up in the debate about cause. It shows up in the sequence of our attention. And that sequence has nothing to do with the science. It has to do with us. And there is an industry whose entire business model is that sequence. There is a market whose product is your dread, and it does not get paid when the answer turns out to be complicated. The market for parenting books rewards exactly one shape of argument: a single villain, a clean line of cause, and a fix the buyer can perform without ever once turning the lens around. The Anxious Generation spent more than a year on the bestseller list , topping it repeatedly, because that is the shape that sells -- which is a different property from the shape that's true, and the two come apart more often than the sales rank will ever admit. This doesn't require a single cynic. No author has to be insincere for it to work. The market selects the scary-single-cause book the way the mall selects the impulse buy -- automatically, structurally, by rewarding the version that moves. Sincerity is beside the point, and that's exactly what makes it structural rather than a cheap shot: the incentive bends the whole conversation whether or not anyone at the keyboard means to bend it. Here's the rhyme. The externalizing book sells because it externalizes. It's the same test I'm about to put to everything else -- who pays? -- run at the scale of an entire industry, and the industry picks the cop-out every single time, because the cop-out is the product. A book titled It's Partly You, and Here Is the Expensive List does not move units. So the scary book isn't describing the easy solution. It is one -- an external enemy, a clean story, relief from self-examination, twenty-eight dollars with free returns. The diagnosis is the dopamine. The parent closes the cover feeling armed instead of implicated, and feeling armed is precisely the sensation that prevents the costly change. And I have to say the next part louder than any of it, because I'm standing in this exact market. I write a Substack. I'm writing a book. I am producing words about technology and children inside the same economy I'm describing. The only honest defense against my own argument is to be the rare writer who mails you an invoice instead of a villain -- and to admit, out loud, that the invoice is the harder thing to sell. So here's the test I'm holding myself to in this very paragraph: am I handing you someone to blame, or a bill with my own name at the top? If I ever start selling you fear about AI the way the phone books sell fear about phones, you should close the tab. One discipline, so this doesn't rot into "it's all a grift." The book can contain real evidence and be shaped by a market that would have rewarded it even if it hadn't. The money doesn't make the research fake. The money explains why this shape of argument drowns out the messier, truer one -- the version where the phone is real and the forest was dry and we lit half the matches ourselves. The moment I say "it's all a grift," I've made the exact single-villain move I'm prosecuting. I've just swapped the phone for the publisher. Now spend the rehearsal on opening night. The panic says AI is making kids stop thinking. So ask the question back: were we teaching them to think -- or to perform thinking? Five paragraphs to a rubric. Themes regurgitated on cue. The thesis statement in the assigned position. The essay as ritual, gameable for decades by any kid with a good memory and a sense of what the teacher wanted to hear. If the assignment was already a performance, then AI didn't kill thinking. It revealed that we'd been grading the performance all along and calling it cognition. The essay was always counterfeitable. AI just made the counterfeiting free, and instant, and impossible to ignore. I'll grant the disanalogy, because it's the best objection and it's real: AI isn't perfectly like television. The kid watching the wasteland still went and wrote his own essay afterward. AI does the assigned cognition itself. That's a real difference -- and it cuts my way, not against me. Offloading only matters if there was something there to offload. Where the thinking was real, AI can't touch it. Where it was already fake, AI just retires it. So AI is a sorting machine. It kills the counterfeit assignments and leaves the genuine ones standing -- the live, unscripted, defend-your-claim-against-a-human-in-real-time kind, the kind a model can't sit in for you. And here's the tell: the panic is loudest exactly where the assignments were always counterfeit. The crisis was never that the machine can do the work. The crisis is that the machine can do the work and no one can tell the difference -- and that was true about the assignment before the machine ever showed up. We would rather build a detector to protect a broken assignment than admit the assignment was broken. The detector is the confession. Which brings us to the test the whole thing turns on. Why the ban? Why always the ban? Not because we're lazy, and not because we're cowards. Because the ban is the only intervention on the entire menu that costs the adults proposing it nothing. Watch what every honest alternative actually bills us. We taught to the test -- so fixing it means killing the high-stakes regime, and the price is surrendering the clean number that funding, accountability, and college sorting are all calibrated to. Nobody wants to give up the metric, even while admitting it's deforming the kid. We sold a four-year degree we already knew was inflating -- so fixing it means telling kids the truth about credentials, and the price is that the people who'd have to tell that truth are employed by the thing they'd be telling the truth about. We locked the doors and scheduled every hour out of safetyism -- so fixing it means handing autonomy back, and the price is tolerating that a kid gets hurt and it isn't automatically a lawsuit. We modeled compulsive use at our own dinner tables -- so fixing it means putting our own phones down, which is the cheapest thing in the world to say and the most exposing thing in the world to do. Every one of those sends the invoice to the adult. The ban sends the invoice to the child. That is why it's a cop-out -- not because we failed to look, but because we looked, priced the honest options, and chose the one we don't have to pay for. So here's the test, and it's sharper than any amount of exhortation: look at any proposed fix and ask who pays. If your remedy for the kids is something the kids have to do -- get off the phone, stop using the chatbot -- and nothing you have to do, you've found the cop-out. And it has your fingerprints on it. And the institution has noticed the fear, and it has a product for it. The school steps forward as savior. Give us your child, and we'll protect them from the digital age. The phone pouch at the door. The AI-detector subscription. The screen-free pledge. The assembly with the guest speaker about the dangers of the feed. And parents are grateful -- because gratitude is the point of the transaction. But look at what's actually being sold. The protection is a promise to rebuild a world that no longer exists and seal the child inside it: a walled garden modeled on the childhood the adults had, which is the one world the kid is guaranteed never to live in. The school cannot deliver a pre-digital adulthood, because there isn't one to deliver. The graduate walks out the gate into the exact world the pouch pretended away. The screen-free campus isn't preparation. It's a diorama. And the same move runs from the opposite direction -- the district racing to teach AI, the one-to-one laptop, the innovation lab, the future-ready brochure. Opposite gestures, identical transaction. The panic room and the rocket ship are the same booth, and the only question either one actually answers is which fear is selling better this quarter. We already caught the publisher selling parents a villain. The school is in the same business -- it has simply productized the relief. The pouch, the pledge, the detector: these are the institutional version of the twenty-eight-dollar book, sold not for money but for the thing a school needs more than money -- the parent's faith that someone competent is handling it. And the relief works the same way it works in the bookstore. The parent who watched the phones get locked away goes home feeling the problem is managed -- and feeling managed is exactly what forecloses the harder conversation, the one about the test regime and the credential lie and the status culture, all of it still running, untouched, behind the pouch. The pouch doesn't fix the room. It furnishes the room, so nobody asks why they're in it. Two disciplines, because this one curdles into school-bashing faster than anything else, and the people reading this are the school. First: aim at the institution as a system, never at the teacher, and not even at the principal who bought the pouches in good faith believing it was the responsible thing. The school reaches for the saleable cure for the same reason the author and the parent do -- because the honest alternative sends it a bill it cannot pay. The real fix would force the institution to say out loud that the assignment was already broken, the test was already deforming the kid, the credential it's selling is already inflating -- and no institution can say that sentence and keep functioning. So it sells the pouch instead. The pouch is the school's cop-out for the identical reason the ban is the parent's: it's the cure that costs the institution nothing and changes nothing it would have to change about itself. Second, the "and," not the "or." Some phone limits in schools are genuinely defensible. A focused classroom is a real good, and I'll lose you instantly if I sneer at every pouch as pure theater. The knife isn't "limiting phones is fake." The knife is the savior posture -- the promise to protect kids from the digital age sold as a substitute for preparing them for it. A school can lock the phones during fourth period and be dead honest that it cannot wall a child off from the century they will graduate into. Cut the salesmanship. Keep the practice. So what would the honest version cost -- specifically, and with my own name on it? Because if I leave this abstract, I've just written the greeting-card version of the exact thing I've spent two thousand words prosecuting. "Take responsibility" is the cheapest line on the menu. Here's the bill. Put my phone face-down at dinner and in the car -- not as a rule I impose on them, but as a practice I hold,
